name: Facial Autologous Muscular Injection (FAMI)

lead: FAMI is a facial fat-grafting approach in which a person's own fat is injected into facial muscle to restore volume and contour, giving a fuller, more contoured face. A 2007 review lists it with lipostructure and facial fat rebalancing as newer concepts for three-dimensional rejuvenation of the whole face.

Fat is harvested from elsewhere on the body and injected into facial muscle, as the name describes. Little else is published on it specifically, and the same review notes that practical ways to measure fat-transfer outcomes objectively are lacking.

paras: It is a clinic procedure done by a surgeon, with fat taken from one area of the body and placed in the face. Swelling settles over days to weeks, and part of the fat may be reabsorbed before the final result.
General fat-grafting references list swelling, bruising, haematoma, contour irregularities, infection and partial reabsorption of the fat. FAMI-specific safety data were not found.

chain: Own fat injected into facial muscle
angle.text: The payoff is restored volume and a fuller, more contoured face using the patient's own fat. Fat is harvested and injected into facial muscle. A 2007 review lists it among newer fat-transfer concepts, and little is published on it specifically.

lead: Facial Autologous Muscular Injection (FAMI), or fat autograft muscle injection, is a facial fat-grafting technique in which a patient's own fat is injected into the muscles of facial expression to restore volume and contour.[1][2] It was developed by Roger E. Amar, and is used for full-face or regional volume, for example in the cheeks, chin and perioral area.[2][3]

The aim is a fuller, softer and more proportioned face, such as a better-defined chin and jaw border after neck liposuction. The technique places fat inside muscle to maximize survival of the fat cells, which the first descriptions say addresses the unpredictable longevity and asymmetry of conventional fat grafts.[1][2]

Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series: 100 patients in 2003, 30 patients treated with neck liposuction in 2003, a 2005 technique description and a 2011 paper in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery, plus a 2007 review that lists FAMI among newer full-face rejuvenation concepts and notes that objective outcome measures are lacking.[4][1][2][3][5][6]
infobox: Autologous fat grafting into facial muscle

paras: As described in 2005, fat is gently harvested and centrifuged for three minutes, loaded into small syringes and placed with blunt cannulae shaped to fit muscle contours. Fat is injected into the muscle along its length in a retrograde fashion, and either the full face or regions may be treated.[1]

The rationale given is that conventional fat grafts had shown asymmetry and transient duration, and that large-volume injection for panfacial correction could cause edema lasting months; placing fat within muscle is intended to maximize adipocyte survival.[1][2]

Fat grafting in general has three stages, according to Wikipedia: harvesting fat, usually by liposuction; processing it; and reinjecting the purified fat. The article stresses that grafts should not be handled excessively and should be reinjected quickly to preserve them, and that the procedure can be done under local or general anaesthesia [7]. FAMI differs from conventional grafting by the plane of placement: the fat is deposited within the muscles of facial expression rather than only in the subcutaneous layer [1][2].

Wikipedia describes the usual donor areas as the hip, knee or abdomen, curved disposable cannulas that follow the skull contours so no incisions are needed, and an outpatient procedure under local anaesthesia.[5]

In a 2003 series of 100 patients, volumes of 3 to 63 cc of centrifuged fat were injected in one session, with no complications reported, downtime of 5 to 7 days, high patient satisfaction and follow-up of 3 to 6 months.[2]

In a 30-patient series combining submental tumescent liposuction with FAMI, all patients improved in the cervicomental border, mandibular border smoothness and chin proportion after 3 to 5 days of swelling; those followed for 6 to 12 months had long-term fat retention and no significant complications.[3]

A 2011 paper by Amar and Donald Fox in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery presented three illustrative cases from the lead author's experience of about 700 patients over 10 years. It describes FAMI as an anatomically targeted approach to facial fat grafting, links grafting into the muscles of facial expression to improved graft retention, predictability and symmetry, and reports that 80 to 90 percent of cases needed only one session.[6]

A 2007 review describes fat augmentation as safe, relatively inexpensive and readily available, and says surgeons increasingly recognise that facial aging reflects tissue atrophy as well as gravity, making fat for volume restoration more popular.[4] General references list swelling, bruising, haematoma, contour irregularity, infection and injury to underlying structures as fat-grafting complications, with some fat reabsorbed over time.[7]
Complications listed for fat grafting also include paraesthesia, donor-site pain, hypertrophic scarring and fat necrosis [7].

Facial fat grafting is used for restoring volume to deflated facial compartments including the periorbital area, and the broader fat-transfer family also covers breast reconstruction and augmentation, gluteal augmentation, hand rejuvenation, rhinoplasty contour correction and scar or burn improvement [7]. Within that family, FAMI is aimed at the cheeks, chin, perioral region or the whole face, and the 2005 description presents it as suited to panfacial correction because the muscle placement is meant to limit the months-long swelling reported with large-volume subcutaneous injection [1]. Wikipedia notes adipose-derived stem cells are thought to contribute to tissue-quality improvements after grafting, and observes that the body may reabsorb up to about half of transferred fat in breast augmentation, which illustrates why graft survival is a central concern for all fat-transfer techniques [7].
Wikipedia treats FAMI as a variant of facial fat grafting, with fat deposited deep in multiple planes rather than only under the skin.[7][5]

Studies are case series from the developer's practice and colleagues: 100 patients with 3 to 6 months of follow-up, 30 neck-liposuction patients followed up to a year, a technique description and a 2011 case-based paper with about 700 patients in the lead author's experience.[1][2][3][6] No randomised or independently conducted controlled trials of FAMI have been published. A 2007 review notes that practical means of objectively measuring fat-transfer outcomes are lacking and that questions remain about optimal harvest site, processing and injection technique.[4]

timeline.event: Roger E. Amar begins developing FAMI.[5]
FAMI is introduced in the United States.[5]
A 100-patient series of the FAMI technique, developed by Roger E. Amar, is published in Dermatologic Surgery.[2]
A 30-patient series pairs FAMI with submental liposuction.[3]
FAMI is described as a new technique for facial volume restoration.[1]
A review lists FAMI among newer full-face rejuvenation concepts.[4]
FAMI is introduced in London; Amar, Fox and Balin publish a cadaver study on cannulation of facial expression muscles.[5]
Amar and Fox publish a FAMI procedure paper in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery.[6]
